Short but surprisingly relaxing!

It's a bummer how short the story really is (only five chapters to the story), because this was a beautifully crafted game! Despite the content, the interface of the game and minimal soundtrack made for a calming gaming experience. Choices can make or break your ending, and I applaud the idea of uploading information within it's context (something frequently missed in real life, unfortunately.)

Even after completing each ending, I would certainly return to this game again to play through it. Personally I wouldn't mind trying the game if it had a freeplay mode outside of its story mode (a la Endless Mode in Papers Please), but the current version was still a delight to play!

Stay vigilant, inspectors!

There are many identities that you can choose at the start of the game.
I chose to become a grandma.
On the internet, no one knows you're a grandma.

Jokes aside, Orwell captures what I love most about indie games: a simple idea that invokes thoughts and feelings.

Orwell provides a nice overview of the current state of our privacy: constantly surveillanced, seldom noticed.
I backed two other similar games on Kickstarter (Top Secret and Need To Know) wishing for the same thing I can feel playing this game: the responsibility (or the lack thereof) of spying on other's privacy, and deciding how they should be looked at or dealt with: a small oversight on a character's relationship status could make me think about it till the end of the game. Even though such details may not be important to the story, it still bothered me: because it is the identity that I altered, and there was no turning back. It fits well with doublethink, and made me Winston: I might be the only one who knows the truth that he is divorced, but to everyone else, he is still married (this circumstance did not sound familiar until I wrote that line down, makes me curious if the given decision is put in delibrately). And this thought is freightening; because "he might be alone in holding that belief, and if alone, then a lunatic... the horror was that he might also be wrong." This thought of people not caring about this as it serves no function, and the possibility that I might be actually wrong and it really does not matter, troubles me greatly.

The mechanics are similar to what workers do at Recdep, but of course not entirely, as the purpose of Recdep does not fit the current state of politics nor the theme of this game. Instead of altering history, we are 'phrasing' history, finding quotes which can be used for our advantage and possibly against our target, the quotes may not need to be said seriously or truthfully, nor are they meant to be always perceived literally, but we use them all the same: perhap an alternate form of "the indifference of reality". Although not altering history in any way, you are still creating history, and that is very doublethink.

Choices. Whether this is not Ingsoc is debatable, as there are preferable choices and crimethink for Ingsoc. However, choices in Orwell definitely allow the player to be as Orwellian as they wish to be, in terms of accusations. You can charge a person with crime from a single sentence and thought, some may not even be said seriously. Of course, Orwell needs to allow you the freedom of choice, because our current state of freedom allows it, or as we think. Nevertheless, the ultimate choice is still yours. In my first playthrough I decided to unbellyfeel my superior. Perhaps I will do something else next time.

Overall, this game at least is able to capture the Orwellian idea of possible surveillance and control, while attempts to inform the players that we may still have the ultimate power of choice. Whether of not this game will still ring true 4 years later is uncertain for me at the moment, but as a person who loves Nineteen Eighty-Four, I am happy to see that people can make an effort to prove that oldthinkers unbellyfeel Ingsoc.

(4 years later: fortunately not)

Great game, and a good story. I have never had a game that would make me doubt myself on how chose my decission. It actually felt as if I was twriling peoples lives in my hand with the way I was using the information i dug up on each character.

Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

Each "episode" in Orwell for me was about 45 minutes to an hour long, including the first episode (which isn't shown in time played because I played the first episode in the demo), and they are very fun. I LOVED this game. I don't play these kinds of games alot, either. I mostly play FPS games. But Orwell was amazing. The art style is unique, and I really liked it. When you see important pieces of information, the music that plays makes it so much more dramatic, and you can really sense the tension behind what is going on in the story. In Orwell, you play as the Investigator. You were invited to the Orwell program, which is a surveillence system that allows you to go through websites online and extract information from a suspect. Throughout the game, you begin to question whether what you are doing is right, and who exactly are the "good guys" and the "bad guys." You have to be careful about which information you upload to the Orwell database (because only you can see ALL the information, so some of it you upload may be put out of context) because it might not be the correct information. It's a game that tests your morality, and, at the end, surprises you. The person I thought who wasn't the bad guy turned out to be the bad guy. So overall, I LOVED this game sooooo much. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone, because if someone like me who plays mostly FPS games can love this, then anyone can love this game.

Orwell does well in what most text based games do and that's writting a decent story. I would even say somewhat enthralling. There's sound triggers and shit that make your heart jump a bit when you come across some real juicy information. Skipping around the different characterps and following their chats, accessing their PCs, etc is all fun and shit. My only complaint is that I felt like I wasn't in quite as much control as I'd like to have been. Probably a bit too linear for the kind of story they're trying to tell and the role you play in that story. I'd would like to have had more options. Which is DOES give you a fair amount of information to jungle but I felt in the end it all went to nothing.

Verdict - good game, good soundtrack, good story, good characters. Gameplay was a too linear.
Will recommend but may not play again. We'll see.

As a newly appointed investigator, you are tasked with bringing the far-reaching powers of the Orwell spying system to try and find the perpetrator of a bombing. As you delve deeper into the lives of those upon whom you spy, you will face choices about how far you should go in your pursuit of National Security.

The game uses a simple drag and drop mechanism for reporting information, yet you will have to use your powers of inference and deduction for when a computer cannot detect nuance. 

I found this game to be a lot of fun, and a little corrupting. It is too easy to spy upon people and one begins to feel justified in reporting every potentially threatening thought they might utter. Recommended if you like your games with a deeper level of story and investigation.

It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

8.2/10.

I saw someone complaining that they didn't enjoy the game because it asks for an email address at the start. I would like to point out that this is optional and has no effect on the game, at all.


Pros:

- I love 1984 and obviously this game is heavily inspired by it.
- Relaxing gameplay.
- Thought-provoking story, especially as we seem to be moving towards a world of 'alternative facts' and other Orwellian concepts in real life.
- Game is long enough that I felt like I got my money's worth, but not so long that it started to get boring and overstay its welcome.
- Seems to have enough replay value for at least two playthroughs.
- Is not too heavy-handed with the anti-surveillance message. Clearly that is the point of the game, but they don't treat you like an idiot with it.
- Some of the choices do require actual thought and planning to make the right choice.
- Consequences for making the wrong choices.
 
Cons:

- In my opinion, the artsyle is a bit too 'whimsical' for the plot of the game. They seemed at odds with one another most of the time.
- It would have been nice if there had been some voice acting. I didn't mind that most of the game was just text, but when listening on phonecalls it would have been nice for them to have been voiced with subtitles.
- The story is extremely linear where one piece of located text triggers the next event and nothing will happen until you find it. Once you realize this it does take some of the urgency out of the game. It would be nice if things like IM chats and phone calls happened whether you were ready or not, so that there could be some threat of you missing information or getting swamped.
- The game holds your hand the entire way. When I first booted it up I thought that I was in a tutorial segment and that a while the highlighting around relevant text and the constant prodding from your supervisor would slow down, but they don't. Every bit of important information is highlighted for you already, so you really don't have to read anything if you don't want to. In a way the game will play itself in a way. There are times when you can choose the wrong info and get scolded, but I found that 95% of the time you just upload whatever data Orwell has already highlighted for you. It eliminates the biggest part of the gameplay, in my opinion. I think the game would have benefitted a lot from taking a Papers, Please approach where you have to scour the data and decide what you think is important and your supervisor chimes in every now and then to punish or praise you, depending.

A beautiful and thought-provoking game with a surprisingly deep and complex plotline. The game is very short (around 3-4 hours) but that's not necessarily a bad thing. I didn't expect a simulation game such as this to offer any suspense, excitement or meaningful plot twists but it managed to do just that. All in all an indie game well worth 10 of your local monetary units! Thanks for the experience, Osmotic, can't wait to see what you do next!
This game is great, It's most certainly a game that should've stoodout from the end of 2016. I really want to go further into the description but that would begin to spoil the game. A MUST PLAY!

Story: I would have preferred if not everything was an interconnected web from the beginning. Instead of your first case being THE case, I personally would have found it more entertaining if there were several smaller cases that indirectly lead to a grand finale with the primary case. It would have extended the game a bit and given you a greater sense of accomplishment in my opinion.

Still these are just nitpicks, I got my money's worth out of this game and that's what's important.

This game is a pretty neat take on the "actual computer as game interface" genre made famous by (the much better) Her Story, and it is a provocative take on government spying as well. The gameplay itself is fun and interesting, but not nearly as deep as it could be. Unlike in Her Story, I rarely felt like I was truly investigating; between the red highlights, the prompts from your handler, and the linear structure of the investigation itself, I more often than not felt like the game was just leading me along by the nose. Indeed, the prompts from the handler almost ruin the whole experience - in addition to giving you several totally unnecessary hints, he often comments on the investigation itself in ways that are very disruptive and eye-rolly (i.e. "wow, what a strange development!"). I'd rather just be allowed to form opinions on the narrative myself, thank you very much, but unfortunately he cannot be turned off. 

Still, it is definitely worth checking out, especially for its price point. I particularly enjoyed the social network mapping mechanic, the way that you gradually see the connections build between all the people you are investigating. Overall, the game could have been much better, but still a decent game.
I wish it was more clear/easier to be subversive and still progress without spoilers. Interesting idea and brilliant execution nonetheless.

Orwell is an interesting game that places you as an investigator working through an intelligence platform known as Orwell. Through Orwell you will begin to examine facts regarding people's lives which will further enable you to investigate them by gaining access to their bank records, phone calls and other electronic devices that may give you an insight into a terrorist network.

Through this investigation you'll get to know the people closer than regular law-enforcement ever could which will enable you to prevent the loss of lives... but at what price? You will have to decide how far into a person's privacy you are willing to go in order to ensure the safety of others. 

Moral choices. Gotta love 'em.

An interesting but short (5h) game. The game starts fairly strong (questioning the ethics of detaining suspects based on quote mined wiretaps), but gets a lot worse as the developers try to present objectively guilty mass murderers as the "victims" of state surveilance. 

After that point, I simply couldn't take any of the characters seriously any more because they blamed the player character for an armed mass murderer (who chose to resist arrest knowing fully well that security services would be forced to use lethal force)  being killed resisting arrest. 
The game became  an exercise in scrolling of the ravings of assorted lunatics to until the data chunks light up in blue because any sympathy I might have had for them was completely gone. 

It's also unfortunate that quite a few of the data chunks are outright trolling - for example, one data chunks allows you to add Alice being friends with Bob to Alice's profile, but only if you also flag Alice for admitting to torture (because Orwell doesn't understand hyperbole?). You have to decide which of the two obviously wrong options (falsely incriminate Alice for torture, or hide the relationship) is less wrong. 
The addition of some non-insane options (e.g. upload the relationship without the joke about torture) would have been nice.

Absolutely recommend this game. Amazing story telling and you easily get lost in the story and choices actually do matter. This game will make you feel conflicted and put your moral believes in question. I would say this game is better than the walking dead.

Orwell is a very good game. It's very unique in its own way, and even though there isn't really a gameplay per se, it is very entertaining. The story is original and it definetely made me feel torn about my thoughts on the whole situation.

It's a game about reading. Don't expect to be able to do any other thing other than read A LOT and pick what information you think is important to advance the story. If you don't like reading, absolutely do not buy this! If you do, go ahead! The information you pick is important, since it determines the outcome of the story, which is also a plus. Definetely recommend it!

But in the ending, you have a limited number of uploads, a MASSIVE red herring, and have no idea what "dirrection" you need to go to acomplish anything.

Such good potential... TURNED TO CRAP. Your "boss" will tell you EVERYTHING to do and to think. Only much later you will learn that there are data you shouldn't upload if you want things A or B to happen. There are times too where you need to make choices COMPLETELY BASED ON GUESSING, BECAUSE THERE IS NO WAY TO DRAW A LOGIC CONCLUSION ON WHAT IS THE RIGHT CHOICE. Example: The game asks you to get an address from a person. You get two addresses, having NO CLUE OF WHICH ONE IS RIGHT. Ridiculous

But the worst is the ending. You just get thrown in the middle of everything without having a fucking clue of what is going on and I triggered an ending completely by accident because I didn't fucking even know what I was doing

DAMN, this game makes me angry because it could have been so good, but the producers FUCKED IT UP. Don't buy this, seriously. It could have been a great story (the story is actually quite good and made me want to know more), but the ending is a MESS.

This is a difficult one to critique because whether or not you like it is mainly dependent on whether you like the narrative and how it is told. I’m not going to pretend that I know a huge amount about a good story well told, so when it comes to my thoughts on said story, take them with a grain of salt. Before I discuss that though, let’s talk about the game a bit.

[h1]“Interactive” Story[/h1]

In context, you are supposed to be a sort of investigator searching for clues about persons of interest via their emails, social media feeds, and phone conversations. I wouldn’t use the word “investigate” to describe the gameplay. Every import piece of information is already highlighted for you and you just need to drag-and-drop them to the appropriate location. When it comes selecting which documents you want to search through, there are indicators that tell which ones have important data-chunks. You don’t really have to read through the documents and phone texts unless you want story context.

This does streamline the gameplay experience, though. With a lot of story based adventure or point-and-click games, there is a risk of getting stuck at one part and losing all immersion in indirection proportion to mounting frustration. Orwell doesn’t have this problem as it is always very clear where you are supposed to look and this keeps a smooth pacing. As I mentioned earlier, this does contribute to the whole experience not feeling much like a traditional game as it feels much more like a guided tour of the characters and narrative progression. Perhaps a system where you have to highlight pieces of text you feel are important, and if you got the right piece then the story could progress? That may have been the original idea, but that could lead to many frustrations if you just barely missed the part of a quote you were supposed to get.

The only real gameplay in here is when there are two pieces of data that conflict with each other and you have to decide which one to submit to your superior. This could come in the form of two phone conversations by a character where one conversation makes him sound violent and the other makes him sound peaceful. Which one you submit will determine if that character gets arrested later in the story. This factors into a bit of a moral choice system regarding whether you try to paint the main characters and virtuous activists or terrorists. I feel an opportunity was missed to have more greatly divergent storylines to make the player feel like they have a real impact on the world. As it stands, your decisions only change minor events and what ending you get, with most of the heavy decision making existing in the last episode only.

[h1]Interactive “Story”[/h1]

With everything I’ve had to say about the gameplay thus far, you may be a bit perplexed as to why I recommend Orwell. Once again, this isn’t a typical [i]game[/i]. It’s a story with a bit more user control over the pace at which you progress through it. So how is the story?

Pretty good, actually.

The subject matter: government surveillance, is very topical and the game does a good job of showing the many different angles and opinions that people have about it. From those that try to peacefully discuss the issue, publicly criticize it, or are indifferent to it, every character seems believable and for the most part are consistent. The plot is revealed at a steady pace and is able to constantly engage. Appropriate music cues help to reinforce when something drastic has just taken place or when a particularly important piece of data is discovered and it does a good job of drawing you in. The last episode starts to deteriorate when the story starts to massively diverge and the amount of documents and computers to search through becomes overwhelming compared to the rest of the story.

While the data chunks are the most important piece of the story, there is a lot of text to sift through and it fleshes out the characters and game world quite well. A lot of it is unnecessary and for a while I thought that a small sub-plot about terrorism in another country was going to turn out to be a major plot device because the game kept bringing it up, but that ended up being nothing important. Also, documents and conversations are never deleted, so you are free to browse through them at your leisure and one small link could lead you down a rabbit’s hole worth of information. Having assessed these can be handy if the story calls for you to investigate those links and you’re already familiar with them, which does occasionally make you feel like a real investigator.

There are a few off moments when the characters don’t feel believable because we only see them communicate via text. Towards the end, [spoiler]everyone is panicking because they have discovered the Orwell system and can’t figure out how to deal with it,[/spoiler] and sometimes text just isn’t the best way to convey those sorts of emotions. These are hardly deal breakers though because what it boils down to is that whenever I would start the game up, it wasn’t because I felt some obligation to finish it. It was because I wanted to know what happens next. And no matter how many trivial nit-picks I have with the story, that single fact means I have to acknowledge that the story is engaging.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Orwell is a story, and not much of a game. Whatever gameplay is present serves entirely to incrementally progress you through the story and not present any kind of and challenge by itself. An experience like this lives and dies on whether or not its story is engaging which, to me at least, it certainly was.

Now Orwell is a game I've never really seen before, and honestly its very unique and knows how to grab your attention! This is one of the best indie games I've played (I don't play many)

What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

This was a very enjoyable little game, and pretty fairly priced at just £7. I found it in an article in PC Gamer magazine and decided to give it a go, being a big fan of George Orwell's strong writings myself. This game is surprisingly tense and fast paced at times, while at other times the story can be kind of slow. The thing is, this game shows the player the whole "Big Brother State" issue from the other side, you get to see reports of terrible events you could have stopped and it really hit me very hard.

This is a game that has obviously taken real events into consideration as much as Orwell. The undertones in The Nation and the leadership by The Party feels like it would work well as a prequel to one of Orwell's most famous works, Nineteen Eighty-Four, which was so influential it even got a big screen adaptation and starred a great cast for the time including a very young John Hurt. But I digress. The storyline is based around a crowd-surveilance computer interface called Orwell and is brought about in secret after The Party passes the Secrecy Bill. I won't spoil anything about the investigation, but the Bill is very reminiscent of British PM Theresa May's highly controversial Snooper's Charter.

The fact is, the game has this utopian near-future look while having tense feelings of underlying political risk to every act. The five chapters work pretty well to split them up, and the way the interface works is really nice. Every part of the investigation manages to have a consequence, but it leads to the same kind of point in the end. So, in Conclusion:

Pros:

1) Excellent storyline with strong characters and some really tense chapters, such as Nina's storyark (that was both intense and really threw me off, again one you'll have to see for yourself) and the antics of Initiate.

2) An interface that really makes you feel like the investigator.

3) Attention to detail - the game doesn't hold back with its attempts at realism.

4) A real feeling of influence and a concern that this game may be showing the future.

Cons

1) The lack of potential for follow-on sequels - The game ends on a sort-of final note, as you'll find out if you play it.

2) CCTV or Camera Footage actually plays very little part in the game, with text being very dominant. Would be nice have to access event footage, more access to records in the hands of actual authorities and the like to even out the fact it is a government project, not a bedroom-hacker.

3) The length of the game could be greater, If a longer sequel appeared I would certainly want to buy it!

4) Finally, the route taken is too narrow. This game is meant to show the full potential and range of issues a Big Brother style investigation would have, so more routes for different events would create greater depth and realism, as well as adding replayablity.

So, I thoroughly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good who-done-it with a political/ sci-fi twist. 100% a decent little game!

Personally I wouldn't hesitate to give this game 10/10. Loved the concept, loved the gameplay, and the story is one of the best I've played, it's so cleverly written. 

Who the game is for: 
Anyone who likes an excellent story well told with plenty of twists and red herrings
Anyone who likes games that give a message but don't shove it down your throat
Anyone who likes games with consequences to your actions
Anyone who just likes the thought of snooping characters emails, blogs, computers etc
Anyone who digs dystopian near future fiction and conspiracies, or who likes to solve a good mystery.

Who the game is not for: (although I would recommend it to anyone with an open mind)
Anyone who only enjoys action/platforming/FPS/RTS (I like all these, but this game is nothing like them, I guess that's obvious though!)
Anyone with no patience, who doesn't like reading in games, or spending the time to really dig into things.

The price (even not on sale) is more than fair for the depth and work that has gone into making this mini masterpiece (if you rush through, you could spend maybe 4 hours, if you take your time and try and dig into all the information, closer to 8-9 hours). It really pushes the boundaries of story telling within games, and the thrill of coming up with ideas, possibilities, then to change them totally (or not) based off of a piece of information you didnt think was relevant earlier is a real highlight). 

As someone else has said in their review, don't do too much digging into the story before playing, approach the game with an open mind and allow the story and gameplay to take root, play the game your own way.  

Basically, if anything at all about the trailers or game information intrigues you, I wouldnt hesitate to recommend it. You won't regret it.

I've had bad experiences with plot-heavy games. Even Telltale's much celebrated titles did very little for me and have contributed to this theory I've had for a long time to video games, in general, seemed incapable of telling a good story. I've always believed that games were much stronger when focusing on mechanics, and those that sacrificed mechanics in favor of plot would always just create an inferior work compared to books or movies.

Orwell is an exception.

What at first might strike you as a fairly preachy "topic of the day" game managed to surpass all my expectations. From the beginning till the end, Orwell and it's characters captivated me.

Orwell is an elegant game. One that understands perfectly how to integrate the agency of it's players to fit into the narrative it's trying to weave, and does so well. Despite the fact that you simply play as a man behind a computer screen, your actions feel like they have consequences, even if sometimes those consequences are ones you don't intend. The longer I played the game, the more I thought about the consequences of every piece of information I submitted, pouring over every bit of data and agonizing over the tiniest nuances of dialogue

While Orwell's themes should be fairly evident from it's title and presentation, I found the plot to be intelligent and far from one-dimensional. Playing the game, often I thought to myself: "Did I make the right call?", "Should I really have told them about that?" I spent a good thirty minutes trying to decide on what I would do during the ending, and even as I write this review I question if I really did the right thing.

To me, that is the hallmark of a good story. One that engages you, makes you feel invested...and above all else; makes you care. It's been a while since I felt so compelled to write a recommendation. But Orwell is one of these games that comes once in a blue moon, and tend to get sadly overlooked. If you couldn't guess already, I highly recommend Orwell. It's one of the best experiences I've had with a story rich game to date, Osmotic Studios has done a fantastic job.

At times preachy and with an abrupt ending [h1]Orwell[/h1] is a barely a game and more a choose your own adventure 'Telltale' style experience that will manage to keep your interest mostly in characters and plot development rather than graphics or "gameplay".

You're an investigator given access to a machine which allows you to hack and spy on mostly all electronic devices people use allowing you to find incriminating or trivial information. Your findings come in the form of 'datachunks', little pieces of text/photos which will help you to progress over the episodic nature of the story. The game has a very interesting plot up until what I considered a very weak ending. Certainly the commentary on government and corporations spying on people is blatantly apparent even from the title of the game and this is one of my major complaints of the game. It's in your face about it and you're constantly reminded of the unethical machinations people will use in order to claim and establish safety in society. A little subtlety and storytelling devices go a long way but Orwell is admittedly very short and therefore a more direct approach is all you're gonna get.

The message the game sends is one I wholeheartedly agree but in Orwell it just feels like it is the [i]only[/i] thing that matters. The characters have fascinating stories which are not properly explored and are left either as filler or comedic relief. Everything is text based so reading the various newspaper articles, websites, social media conversations, is essential into getting into the game. And Orwell succeeds tremendously in that regard. It feels real and it sort of creates a great atmosphere that you're really prying into people's lives, while at the same time trying to solve the mystery.

The game is quite entertaining in that aspect if you're into that sort of thing but unfortunately the ending felt extremely weak. Without going into spoilers, I would have definitely expected and wanted something bigger but at least you do have a choice in how you resolve the matter.

If you're a fan of text/story based games, Orwell offers a sort-of unique approach and theme to the genre but it falls short on properly exploring the theme besides a flat approach to the whole government spying/surveillance. Nonetheless I cannot deny that it was enjoyable to a certain degree and I'd recommend getting this game on sale if possible. There's also a free demo available from the developers which is extremely nice if you want to try the game and something more modern games could use.

Orwell... What can I say... 
I went into Orwell knowing that information quickly becomes a rabbit hole... but I did not think it would become as deep as it became. Every choice, Every action became a thing that you regret. I would liken Orwell to any big name company out there, collecting information, creating a profile then using it for advertisements but this shows what that concept could become.

In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

I suppose Orwell is too easy. You have a supervisor meant to guide you, not only in Orwell but to guide your progress through the main storyline. It is very easy to just scroll down till you see phrases or words highlighted. Trying to find conflicting datachunks quickly to get past. While there is nothing stopping you, Orwell does try to encourage you to read. The many articles and websites you visit build the world as you continually gain access. In a way, the people you investigate brings you into the world as you unknowingly destroy theirs each datachunk at a time. There has been arguments about taking away the automatic highlighting, as why should you be hired if they have a system that does it, but there is too much that one can assume is needed. It could easily become entering random phrases or words till you get it right. So this way of highlighting does take away this confusion of what is and isn't noteworthy in a wall of text or conversations.

[h1]Sound[/h1]
There's limited sounds to Orwell, having background music and computer sounds. The background soundtrack never really changes until something notewrothy and important comes into view. While computer sounds symbolizes actions, such as a sound of a phone for a phone call and a click as datachunks are being entered.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
While you do stare at a screen of your computer, Orwell has an interesting style when it comes to pictures. They build people with polygons. This gives an interesting visual that pops out when surrounded by text and brightening up the screen. The opening cutscene is one of the places that does not primarily showcase this style, going for more of an shaded outline. While the visuals are minimal, it does look appealing.

[h1]Performance[/h1]
Orwell easily runs well. Only having a few seconds of loading in the beginning of each chapter to load everything. There also seems to be a rare bug, not allowing the player to drag or view the preview of the datachunk. Thankfully, the datachunk is not needed to continue with the story, as it persists through the save, so it may only bother those who view it as an important datachunk to include in a profile.

[h1]Revisiting Orwell[/h1]
As said before, Orwell thrives on the first playthrough. After that, you know what's going to happen. You know what choices affects those you were assigned to. That first playthrough may be remembered as you replay, but so everthing major to the story. This is where you should look up guides as more playthroughs are solely for achievements that were off of the course you took. There are a total of three offical endings, all having subtle changed down the road. There's not much replayability but to see the difference the decisions have on the suspects.

[h1]Report[/h1]
+ Art style
+ Convincing characters; can easily be viewed as real people
+ Compelling story

+/- Your choice to see the world of Orwell
+/- Can be seen as constantly holding your hand

- The phone calls and texts are either too slow or too fast. You have to activate the certain call/text for it to start, breaking immersion since no one will wait till you come into the picture. If you are fast enough you can get two calls or texts (or a combination of the two) at the same time since you are likely to look at something else during other playthroughs. 

Orwell is one of those must play games. With the close hitting theme that may soon become reality. With all chapters released, you can easily have 2-3 hours of gamethrough per playthrough depending on how you choose to play. Orwell shows that you are being watched in some ways, even now, and that even you won't have the best interest for others if they have the possibility to be threats to society. Do not be afraid of going into Orwell this late, as I have and I was able to still get the most out of it.

I am writing this as I just finished the game.

Some people say gamers have no life, but those don't know how it is like to see though eyes of someone else. And here you can see how it could feel like to be a person responsible for decisions on which lives of other people depends, base only on uncertain chunks of data.

An episodic story, about the largest public surveillance operation ever. As an investigator, how far will you go, to ensure the safety of your citizens?

This game is very story driven. With that said, it's actually a quite decent piece of storywriting. The whole thing is supplied with lots of manually written pieces of dialogue and information, with believable characters, and an intriquate plot. It's driven by quite simple, but activating gameplay, where you manually make your way through loaths of information. You also have to sort in the information, as the system isn't perfect, and gives you "wrong" information (It's not a bug, it's a test). You alone have to use your wits to solve the puzzle. This is one of the few games that deliver on the promise that "your choices have consequences". Alternative paths gives replayability, but tbh, i'd play it again for just the one i played through on my first try. 

Without spoiling - nothing is as it seems to be. Stay vigilant, stay relevant, and save The Nation.

I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

In [b]Orwell[/b], you sift through emails, blog posts, text messages and transcripts of telephone conversations (the screen shots of security camera feeds were taken from the opening cut scene - you do not have access to video feeds in the game).  Your mission is to selectively pass along information regarding suspected enemies of "The Nation" to law enforcement.  Authorities act upon the information you provide to prevent terrorism and arrest terrorists.

Orwell has very limited re-playability.  The game has a linear storyline, and restarting the game does not introduce new terrorist plots or suspects.  With the possible exception of achievement hunters, I suspect most people will play the game twice: once to explore the story, and another to make earlier game decisions armed with the knowledge of spoilers.

Simply put, Orwell is not a game, but rather an experience to be had. It is a thought experiment masquerading as an investigative interactive story, and I absolutely loved it. I advise anyone from their late teens and up to play, as the purpose and context may fall a bit short for younger audiences. If you have ever enjoyed Aldous Huxley's "Brave New World" or George Orwell's "1984" this is something you should do at least once and is well worth the price.

Note: I forgot to initially boot the game whilst connected to internet, so actual play time is 4-6 hours for the storyline.
